implementation_notes: In modern .NET the mediator role is usually delegated to MediatR: colleagues (controllers, application services) depend on IMediator and send a request or publish a notification instead of referencing each other, while handlers implement IRequestHandler<TRequest,TResponse> or INotificationHandler<TNotification> and are resolved from the DI container - the hub is a dispatcher and the interaction lives in handlers. That replaces the classic mediator that holds colleague references: nothing central knows every participant, the container wires them. Hand-write the classic structure when the coordination is genuinely one object with a small, stable protocol (a dialog controller), or when a dependency-free codebase rules the library out.
pitfalls: Handlers come from the container, so a missing registration fails at runtime where a direct call would not compile; register per assembly and validate registrations at startup.

Publish invokes every INotificationHandler in-process and sequentially on the caller's thread by default, so a slow or throwing handler delays or faults the sender; exception policy and parallelism must be explicit.
Using Send() for what is really a domain notification reintroduces request/response coupling; keep commands and notifications distinct.
Handlers are resolved from a scope: injecting scoped services (DbContext) into a handler resolved from the root scope fails, so the mediator must run inside the request or unit-of-work scope.

variants.name: Classic hand-written mediator (interface + colleague base)
variants.idiom_name: IMediator.Notify(object sender, string evt) + Colleague base holding the interface
variants.implementation_notes: The GoF structure in plain C#: an IMediator interface with a single Notify entry point, a concrete coordinator (often the dialog or controller) holding typed references to the colleagues it coordinates, and colleagues that keep an IMediator reference and report events instead of calling each other. Choose it for a small, stable, framework-free collaboration where adding a library would cost more than the code it replaces; switch to the MediatR variant once the interactions multiply and handlers need central composition or validation.
pitfalls: object sender plus a string event discards the compiler's help; a closed enum or record event type keeps the protocol checked.
The mediator holds concrete colleague types, so every protocol change edits the hub - exactly the coupling that lets a mediator grow into a god object.
Notify runs synchronously on the caller's thread; on a UI thread a blocking handler freezes the interface, so hop to async work deliberately.
